column2: The JVM is specified as an abstract computing machine that knows nothing of the Java language only of the class-file binary format so any language expressible in valid class files can be hosted on it
column10: Language-vs-runtime attribution: hosting property belongs to the VM layer

column2: The JVM spec states it is not inherently interpreted and can be implemented by compiling to silicon; its portability guarantees (hardware/OS independence) are properties of the VM not of Java syntax
column10: Hosting property belongs to the VM layer

column2: .NET compiles all managed languages to language-independent CIL plus self-describing metadata JIT-compiles each method on first call after a type-safety verification step and the same CIL runs on any supported architecture
column10: Metadata removes need for type libraries/IDL

column2: Microsoft documents that JIT compilation affects performance adversely at runtime and that JIT-generated code is bound to one process which is why the NGen ahead-of-time mode exists to persist native code on disk
column10: Vendor admission of JIT cost from primary docs

column2: Oracle documents that HotSpot startup interleaves class scanning/loading/linking/initialization and that large framework server applications may require seconds or even minutes to start up; profiling instrumentation makes JIT-compiled code slower than uninstrumented code during warmup
column10: JEP 483 motivation plus JEP 544 three-phase startup description

column2: JDK 24's AOT cache cut Spring PetClinic startup from 4.486s to 2.604s (42%) using a 130MB cache and JEP 544 (JDK 28) extends this to cached AOT-compiled native code with automatic fallback to JIT; AOT code is not cross-compilable and an AOT-only mode is explicitly a non-goal
column10: Cache validity requires same JDK/arch/OS (reproducibility constraint); cache format subject to change

column2: GraalVM Native Image applies a closed-world assumption: no new code is loaded at run time reflection/resources require build-time reachability metadata and if static analysis cannot prove an element is needed the application can fail at run time
column10: Coordinator spot-check passed; closed-world described as not amenable to all applications

column2: Native Image builds are slow (hello world ~14s in the docs' own example) default to Serial GC with max heap 80% of RAM do not support JVMTI/bytecode-based Java tools and have per-architecture limits (musl unsupported on Linux AArch64)
column10: Version in build output: Oracle GraalVM 24+36.1; docs site 25.x

column2: Build-time class initialization in Native Image executes user code during the build and stores the resulting state in the image heap — e.g. a system property read in a static initializer is fixed into the binary
column10: Docs' own example demonstrates environment baked into binary

column2: .NET NativeAOT forbids dynamic loading and runtime code generation (System.Reflection.Emit) requires trimming and single-file layout pre-generates every struct-generic instantiation which can have significant disk-size impact and ships only limited diagnostics support
column10: Also no C++/CLI; no built-in COM on Windows; binary runs only on same-or-newer Linux

column2: ZGC's stated design goal is pause times not exceeding 1 millisecond independent of heap size achieved by doing collection concurrently via colored pointers plus load/store barriers injected into compiled code
column10: Barriers are a per-access throughput cost mechanism

column2: Generational ZGC applies the weak generational hypothesis; the JEP reports a Cassandra benchmark with 4x throughput at one quarter the heap vs non-generational ZGC while flagging implementation complexity and possible regression for non-generational workloads
column10: Vendor-reported benchmark; no method section; magnitude indicative only

column2: Kotlin coroutines compile to state machines with no special JVM support; they were experimental in Kotlin 1.1-1.2 under a separate experimental package to preserve compatibility and became stable only in 1.3
column10: Async as language/compiler feature rather than runtime feature

column2: Java virtual threads (final JDK 21) implement M:N user-mode scheduling to restore thread-per-request scalability; the JEP states they are not faster threads and exist to provide scale (throughput) not speed (latency)
column10: JEP argues async/callback style costs usable context in stack traces

column2: Kotlin puts nullability in the type system (String vs String?): the compiler rejects direct member access on nullable values and guarantees non-null variables hold valid values
column10: Platform types (Java interop) remain an NPE risk

column2: C# nullable reference types are entirely a compile-time feature: annotations plus null-state analysis produce warnings and the runtime behavior of the program is unchanged
column10: Retrofit design: opt-in per project; warning-based migration

column2: Java generics are erased: JEP 218 describes the current implementation as one class for all reference instantiations with no primitive support causing boxing overhead and pseudo-specialized API proliferation (IntStream; ToIntFunction); the specialization JEP has remained Candidate for over 10 years
column10: JEP lists open retrofit problems: arrays; null; overloading; reflection; inference

column2: Kotlin value/inline classes required name mangling of JVM signatures (since 1.4.30) because the JVM lacks an identity-free value representation
column10: Stable since Kotlin 1.5.0; target JVM shows through as constraint

column2: Swift uses ARC for class instances only (structs and enums are value types); strong reference cycles between class instances cause memory leaks and must be resolved manually with weak or unowned references
column10: ARC eliminates tracing-GC pauses but moves cycle-breaking to the programmer

column2: Swift's ABI manifesto holds that once an ABI is stable it persists for the platform's lifetime and any inefficiencies at that point effectively persist forever; library evolution uses resilient (opaque) layouts
column10: Module format stability as separate requirement for binary frameworks

column2: The Java Platform Module System provides reliable configuration and strong encapsulation but version strings on the module path are ignored and the module system explicitly does not address version selection delegating that to build tools
column10: JPMS compatibility risk listed as primary risk

column2: The FFM API (final JDK 22) replaces JNI's brittleness with pure-Java downcalls with stated goals of JNI-comparable-or-better performance and soundness guaranteeing no use-after-free; JNI's documented flaws include triple-artifact glue and struct/object mismatch
column10: Relates to JEP 472 integrity policy tightening

column2: A real project ported to Native Image (native Minecraft server) reports competitive performance with reduced footprint but documents limitations: no mod support; no GUI; single MC version; startup flakiness
column10: Project testimony; single case

column2: JVM startup criticism is contested: JEPs put large server-app startup at seconds-to-minutes while a practitioner article argues startup time has rarely mattered for long-running server deployments
column10: Scopes differ (CLI/serverless vs long-running server); recorded in conflicting-evidence.md

column2: Hypothesis: if Kavir adopts a managed runtime deciding at v1 between dynamic execution (JIT; reflective; open-world) and closed-world AOT-friendliness will be cheaper than retrofitting the other later
column10: Motivated by C-207;C-210;C-206;C-209; Phase-2 ADR candidate

column2: Hypothesis: putting identity-free value types; non-null types; and an explicit module version-selection policy in Kavir's v1 type system will avoid the decade-scale retrofit costs documented for Java; Kotlin and Swift
column10: Motivated by C-217;C-218;C-221;C-215; Phase-2 ADR candidate
